title: Step Track
description: Find the step between neighbours on a track, carry a number or letter series on, and make a series of your own from a start and a rule.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Find the step from each term to the next, check it all along, and carry a number or letter series on, or make one of your own from a start and a rule.
writeup.look: A track of stepping stones with a jump arc over every pair of neighbours, a letter track under it, and a pairing tray and a rule maker at the side.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only. 'Step Track' sits in ink at the far left, with a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it. The phase title sits beside the dot on the same line, then the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart stand as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the stones filled against the stones this phase leaves blank, two numbers in ink. The first climbs by one as each stone fills or each heap is paired, and the second is fixed at what this phase holds. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score, even on a track that does. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. Stepping stones run across the working area: ten stones, each 96 across with 12 between, at 64,300, reaching 1132. Over every pair of neighbours hangs a jump arc, in the band from 222 to 292, with its label sitting on the arc itself. The step finder fills the labels one at a time from the left, each as the second term less the first. A step up is labelled with an add sign and a step down with a take-away sign. Arc compare lifts any two arcs and stands them side by side in a box 140 by 90 at 600,630, where a difference in length is seen at once. A counting-down track is laid from the right, so it runs towards a zero stone at its left end with nothing drawn beyond it. A step that would pass zero is handed back with the zero stone lit in reddish purple. The letter track runs under the number track: twenty-six small stones, each 38 across with 3 between, at 64,450, reaching 1127. Its own arcs hang in the band from 406 to 446, and the place toggle writes each letter's place in the alphabet in the row from 492 to 516. The pairing tray sits at the lower left, 520 by 190 at 64,530, and takes a heap of up to twenty counters. Pair them sets the counters out two by two at walking pace. Any counter left without a partner stands on its own at the end, in reddish purple. The even or odd card, 140 by 90 at 600,530, turns from what is left. The rule maker sits at the lower right, 400 by 190 at 750,530, and takes a start, or two starts, and one rule from its list. The list holds four rules: add a step, take a step away, add each number to itself, and add the two numbers before. The track then fills stone by stone with every arc labelled as it lands. On the last two rules each new arc is drawn up out of the stones it came from. Down the right of the canvas the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92), which holds what the child has given. That rectangle is the same on every phase and is never animated in or out. Under it is the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a term or a step is asked for, with an add key and a take-away key beside them. On the letter track it becomes twenty-six letter keys, seven across in four rows, with the last row holding five. The even and odd keys stand under both, and on the fourth phase the rule maker's four rules are keys of their own. The footer runs 758 to 900. The voice caption sits at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling. The phase bar sits at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, taken from its pictures. Whatever the stage hands over is deep blue: a given term, a bead, the bottom row of a tower, a plain letter, a tile already laid. The first member of a repeating group is deep blue too, and the second member, or a second kind set beside the first, is amber. The step itself is vermilion in every tool without exception: a jump arc and its label, a quarter turn, an operation sign, a key's shift. Whatever the rule makes is green: a next term, a built box, a coded or decoded letter, a copy just laid, a tick. Whatever the child is asked to notice is reddish purple: a broken box, a closed-in gap, a doubled part, a leftover counter, a line put back. The dots of dotted paper are grey and nothing else is. Every bracket, outline, rule and blank is near-black chrome. Chrome never borrows a content colour, and no content colour is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because a thing is told by its label or its place before it is told by its colour. A blank waiting for the child is an empty outlined box, never a faded copy of its answer. No track is ever drawn running on past its zero stone, and no stone, label or dot is drawn to the left of it. A list printed with dots after its last term says the list goes on, and on this stage a count down that has reached zero has nowhere left to go.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last track the child filled with every jump arc labelled, and the series they built in the rule maker standing under it with its start and its rule written beside it.

phases.win: every arc shows the same label and the blank stones fill one jump at a time
phases.does: labels every arc with the step, checks that they match, then fills the blank stones
phases.goal: the step between neighbours is found, checked all along and used, and a count down stops at zero
phases.says: How far is each jump? Check every one before you go on.
phases.check: Away from the screen: count down from forty in steps of ten. Say the last number, and why it is the last.
phases.feels: every jump the same size, checked all along, and a count down that has somewhere to stop
phases.hands: Chalk a trail of squares in the playground. One child sets a start and a secret step and chalks the first four terms. The next child walks the trail, says the step between every pair aloud, and chalks the next three. Then chalk a trail that counts down by eight from fifty-six, and ask what the last square holds and why nothing comes after it. Counting back in ones is called counting back; use no other name for it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what is the jump between the first two stones? Second rung, the phase's: is it the same between every pair? Third rung: the track is cut to three stones and one blank, and the child labels both arcs before filling it. The number keys stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: the first two terms are the first thing read, and on most tracks the first step is the only step there is.
wrong.move: reads the step off the first pair and carries it on without checking the pairs after it.
wrong.screen: the step finder labels every arc again one at a time from the left, and any arc whose label differs is ringed in reddish purple. The child's stones stay where they were filled. Arc compare stands that arc beside the first, and both stay on the stage.

wrong.why: the list that goes down by fifty ends in dots after fifty, and dots say that a list goes on.
wrong.move: carries a count down on past the zero stone, or stops at the last term printed before it.
wrong.screen: a step that would pass zero is handed back with the zero stone lit, and nothing is drawn to the left of it. Where the child stopped short, the stone before zero stays drawn and open. The count down is then walked from the first term, one jump at a time, to zero, where it stops.

phases.screen: a number track with four terms written and three stones blank, its jump arcs unlabelled
phases.soWhat: Find the step between neighbours, check it for every pair, then keep using it; a count down stops at zero.

phases.win: the next letters light on the track, each with its place in the alphabet beneath it
phases.does: counts the places between neighbouring letters, then steps on by the same amount
phases.goal: letters step along the alphabet the way numbers step along counting
phases.says: How many letters does it jump? Jump the same again.
phases.check: Write the next two letters of C, F, I, and say each one's place in the alphabet.
phases.feels: letters line up like numbers, each with its own place, and a jump along them is counted by its landings
phases.hands: Write the alphabet in a long line across the board and number each letter under it from one. Ask the class to jump from A three letters at a time, touching each landing letter with a ruler and counting the jumps, not the letters passed over. Then write B two, D four, F six, and ask what the numbers have to do with the letters.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many landings from one letter to the next? Second rung, the phase's: what is that letter's place in the alphabet? Third rung: the track is cut to its first ten letters, and the child jumps once with the landings counted aloud. The letter keys stay open.

wrong.why: between A and D there are two letters to see, B and C, and seeing them is easier than counting landings.
wrong.move: counts the letters in between instead of the jump, so A to D reads as a step of two and the track goes on J, L, N.
wrong.screen: the letter track counts the jump from A one landing at a time, lighting B, then C, then D, and numbering each landing. The count stops on the letter it lands on, at three. The child's letters stay on their stones, and the same count is run again from J.

wrong.why: the number step is plain to read, and the letter step is hidden by the letters in between.
wrong.move: steps the letter and its number by different amounts, writing I ten after H eight.
wrong.screen: the place toggle writes each letter's place beneath it, and the child's I stands with nine beneath it, not ten. The jump from H is then counted landing by landing to J, and J's place is written under it. Both letters stay on the track.

phases.screen: the letter track with four letters lit and three places waiting
phases.soWhat: Letters step along the alphabet the way numbers step along counting, and each letter has its place, A as one.

phases.win: the pairs line up and the card turns, with any leftover counter standing on its own
phases.does: sets the counters out two by two and turns the card from what is left
phases.goal: a number that pairs up with none left over is even, and one that leaves one over is odd
phases.says: Put them in pairs. Is anyone left without a partner?
phases.check: Away from the screen: take a handful of beans and put them in pairs. Is your handful even or odd?
phases.feels: the counters line up two by two, and either everyone has a partner or one is left on its own
phases.hands: Hand each pair a heap of buttons, some heaps even and some odd in number. Ask them to set the buttons out two by two, and not to count them first. Then ask whether anyone is left without a partner. Write the counts on the board in two lists, and ask what the class notices about the numbers in each list.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many pairs did the counters make? Second rung, the phase's: is any counter left without a partner? Third rung: the heap is cut to five counters, and the child pairs them one pair at a time. The even and odd keys stay open.

wrong.why: making pairs felt like the whole job, and five pairs were made without any trouble.
wrong.move: calls eleven even because five pairs could be made, without looking at the button left over.
wrong.screen: the pairing tray sets the counters out again two by two at walking pace, and the one left over stands apart at the end in reddish purple. The card waits face down until the leftover has been tapped. The child's answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: a number is read from the left, and the one is the first thing the eye lands on.
wrong.move: calls fourteen odd because its first digit, one, is odd.
wrong.screen: fourteen counters are paired, first a ten making five pairs with none over, then the four making two pairs with none over. Seven pairs stand in a row with no counter left alone. The child's card stays beside the tray.

phases.screen: the pairing tray holding a heap of counters, with an even or odd card waiting
phases.soWhat: A number that pairs up with none left over is even, and one that leaves one over is odd.

phases.win: the next stone fills and its arc is drawn out of the number already reached
phases.does: reads what each step is, fills the next stone, then builds a series of their own from a start and a rule
phases.goal: when the steps are not equal each step is looked at, and a start and a rule make a series of your own
phases.says: The jumps are not the same. Where does each jump come from?
phases.check: Five, ten, twenty, forty. Say where each step comes from, and what comes next.
phases.feels: the jumps grow, and each one is exactly as big as the number the series has already reached
phases.hands: Write six, twelve, twenty-four, forty-eight on the board and ask for the step. Let the class find that the steps are not equal before anyone says why. Then ask where each step comes from, and lay out twelve counters and twelve more to make twenty-four. Each number is added to itself, which is addition the class already has, so name no new rule for it. Finish on the opening page's own task: every child makes a sequence of their own and says its start and its rule.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: are the jumps the same? Second rung, the phase's: how big is each jump next to the stone it starts from? Third rung: the track is cut to two stones and one blank, and the child lays the first stone's counters along the jump. The number keys and the rule list stay open.

wrong.why: the summary box on the same page says number patterns are made by skip counting, and every pattern in the section before this one kept a fixed step.
wrong.move: calls the pattern skip counting and adds the last step again, writing seventy-two after forty-eight.
wrong.screen: the step finder labels the three arcs six, twelve and twenty-four, and arc compare stands them side by side, plainly not equal. Each arc is then drawn up out of the stone it starts from, as long as that stone's number. The child's seventy-two stays on its stone.

wrong.why: the start is the one number that stays in view the whole time, and adding it again looks like keeping to a rule.
wrong.move: in a series of their own made by adding the two numbers before, adds each new number to the start instead, so three, four, seven goes on to ten.
wrong.screen: the rule maker draws two arcs into each new stone, one from each of the two stones before it. The child's ten stands on its stone with its own two arcs, from the start and from the seven. The rule maker's stone lands beside it with its arcs from the four and the seven.

phases.screen: a track whose jump arcs carry different labels, with the rule maker open beside it
phases.soWhat: When the steps are not equal, look at what each step is: here each number is added to itself.
phases.concept: When the steps are not equal

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when a stone fills on a track whose steps are not equal. The number already reached lifts off its stone as a rod of counters, and a copy of the rod lays itself along the next jump, where it fits exactly. The next stone lands at the rod's far end with its number written on it. On a track built in the rule maker from two starts, the rod lifts from the stone two back instead, and fits the jump just as exactly. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a number track stands with four terms written, three stones blank and every jump arc unlabelled. On the second the letter track stands with four letters lit and three places waiting. On the third the pairing tray holds a heap of counters, with the even or odd card face down beside it. On the fourth a track stands whose arcs already carry labels that differ, with the rule maker open at the lower right. The running count at the top left holds the stones filled against the stones this phase leaves blank, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first unlabelled arc, or the first letter, or the heap, or the largest label, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks how far each jump goes. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any start and any rule in the rule maker, on the number track or the letter track, with the pairing tray open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the step between neighbours, letters that step, pairing for even and odd, and series whose steps are not equal, including one the child makes from a start and a rule.
voiceLines: A track of stones, with a jump between each pair. How far is every jump?
How far is each jump? Check every one before you go on.
How many letters does it jump? Jump the same again.
Put them in pairs. Is anyone left without a partner?
The jumps are not the same. Where does each jump come from?
Another track. Check every jump before you fill a stone.
Free play. Choose a start and a rule, and watch the track fill.
Label each jump again from the left, and look for the one that differs.
Every jump labelled, and every series carried on by its own rule.

observations.why: Labels written between every pair of neighbours can be read along the track like a row of their own.
observations.soWhat: Check the step between every pair, not only the first, before carrying a series on.
observations.observe: The step finder labelled every arc, and the one that differed stood out without being looked for.

observations.why: Among the numbers the class counts with, there is nothing below zero to step on to.
observations.soWhat: A series that counts down stops at zero.
observations.observe: The count down reached the zero stone and the next step was handed back.

observations.why: Pairing takes two at a time, so a heap either uses every counter or leaves exactly one over.
observations.soWhat: A number that pairs with none left over is even, and one that leaves one over is odd.
observations.observe: Eleven counters made five pairs, and one counter stood on its own.

observations.why: Each step was the number already reached, so each number was added to itself.
observations.soWhat: When the steps are not equal, look at where each step comes from before guessing the next one.
observations.observe: The arcs of the last track were not equal, and each one was as long as the stone it started from.

phases.screen: a number track with four terms written and three stones blank, its jump arcs unlabelled
phases.win: every arc shows the same label and the blank stones fill one jump at a time
phases.traceback: every arc is labelled again from the left, and the empty stones fill one jump at a time
ladder: What is the jump from the first stone to the second?
Check the jump between the middle stones too.
Start at the stone on the right and find the jump to its neighbour.
Is every jump the same size?
Use that same jump again from the last stone with a number.

phases.screen: the letter track with four letters lit and three places waiting
phases.win: the next letters light on the track, each with its place in the alphabet beneath it
phases.traceback: the hand counts landing by landing along the alphabet and the letter lights with its place written under it
ladder: How many landings does one jump take?
How many landings is it from A to D?
These letters go backwards, so think which way the place goes.

phases.screen: the pairing tray holding a heap of counters, with an even or odd card waiting
phases.win: the pairs line up and the card turns, with any leftover counter standing on its own
phases.traceback: the buttons are set out two by two again, any button left over stands apart, and the card turns to the right word
ladder: Count again at the end of the row and see if anyone is alone.
Do not go by the first digit, but lay all 14 out.
Look at the jump between the stones you can see.
Think in twos and see if anything gets left over.
Odd and even take turns, all the way along.

phases.screen: a track whose jump arcs carry different labels, with the rule maker open beside it
phases.win: the next stone fills and its arc is drawn out of the number already reached
phases.traceback: each jump is laid as a bar beside the stone it starts from, and the next stone fills
ladder: Are the jumps all the same size?
Do the jumps grow or stay the same?
Which two stones does this jump come out of?

items.win: Every jump is 5, so 27 lands next.
Every jump is 6, so 29 fills the stone.

ladder: Take that same jump away again and again, moving left.
Stop at the bar: the end stone is where the count ends.
items.win: Each jump takes 8 away, so 24 is next and the count ends at 0.

ladder: Count the landings from B to D.
Add that many places to the last place you can see.
items.win: Each jump is 2 places, so J at 10 comes next.

ladder: Count B, C, D: one jump is that many landings.
Walk the strip from J and count that many landings.
items.win: Each jump is 3 places, so M comes after J.

ladder: Count the landings from Y back to V.
Take that many places away from the last place.
items.win: Each jump goes back 3 places, so P at 16 is next.
Five pairs and one button left over, so 11 is odd.
Seven pairs and none left over, so 14 is even.
Every jump is 2 and every term is odd, so 39 is next.
ladder: Is every jump the same size?
Each stone has one button left over, so add a whole pair.
Look at the stones behind the jump.
Put each jump beside the stone it starts from.
items.win: Each number is added to itself, and 48 and 48 make 96.

ladder: Compare the first jump with the last one.
Check each jump against the stone it leaves.
items.win: The jump from 72 is 72, so 72 and 72 make 144.

ladder: Look at the two stones just before the empty one.
Add those two stones together.
items.win: 11 comes from adding the 4 and the 7 before it.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: every arc is labelled again from the left, and the empty stones fill one jump at a time
Phase 2: the hand counts landing by landing along the alphabet and the letter lights with its place written under it
Phase 3: the buttons are set out two by two again, any button left over stands apart, and the card turns to the right word
Phase 4: each jump is laid as a bar beside the stone it starts from, and the next stone fills

voice.opening: A track of stones, with a jump between each pair. How far is every jump?
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Choose a start and a rule, and watch the track fill.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: Every jump labelled, and every series carried on by its own rule.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: Write the next three terms of 7, 12, 17, 22.

question.en: What number lands on the next stone after 7, 12, 17, 22?

items.planQuestion: Write the next three terms of 5, 11, 17, 23.

question.en: Which number fills the next stone after 5, 11, 17, 23?

items.planQuestion: Write the next four terms of 56, 48, 40, 32, and say what happens after that.

question.en: It counts down, so what goes on the next stone after 32 and on the end stone?

items.planAnswer: 24, 16, 8 and 0. The step takes away 8 each time, and the count stops at zero

items.planQuestion: Write the next three terms of B2, D4, F6, H8.

question.en: B is at 2, D at 4, F at 6, H at 8, so which place comes next?

items.planQuestion: Write the next two terms of A, D, G, J.

question.en: Which letter follows J in A, D, G, J?

items.planAnswer: M and P, because each letter is three places on from the one before

items.planQuestion: Write the next three terms of Y25, V22, S19.

question.en: Y is at 25, V at 22, S at 19, so what is the next place in this series?

items.planAnswer: P16, M13, J10, because each letter goes three places back and its number is its place in the alphabet

items.planQuestion: Eleven buttons are put into pairs. How many pairs are there, and is eleven even or odd?

question.en: Pair up these 11 buttons, then say if they are even or odd.

items.planAnswer: Five pairs with one button left over, so eleven is odd

items.planQuestion: Fourteen socks are put into pairs. Is fourteen even or odd, and how does pairing show it?

question.en: Pair the 14 socks: is 14 even or odd?

items.planAnswer: Even, because fourteen socks make seven pairs with none left over

items.planQuestion: Write the next three terms of 31, 33, 35, 37, and say whether each term is even or odd.
items.planAnswer: 39, 41 and 43. Each is odd, because adding two adds one more pair and the one left over stays

items.planQuestion: Look at 6, 12, 24, 48. The steps are 6, 12 and 24. What is each step, and what comes next?

question.en: The jumps go 6, then 12, then 24, so what lands after 48?

items.planAnswer: Each step is the number already reached, so 96 comes next

items.planQuestion: Write the next two terms of 9, 18, 36, 72.

question.en: What fills the next stone after 9, 18, 36, 72?

items.planAnswer: 144 and 288. The steps 9, 18 and 36 are not equal. Each step is the number already reached, so each number is added to itself: 72 + 72 = 144 and 144 + 144 = 288

items.planQuestion: Make a series of your own that starts 3, 4 and makes each next number by adding the two numbers before it. Write the next four numbers.

question.en: Each new number is the sum of the two before it: 3, 4, 7, so what comes next?

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

phases.concept: When the steps are not equal

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), terms, arcs, v, i, letterTrack, v, paired, leftOver, start, start, second, b, rule, rule, complete

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves

voiceLines.en: A track of stones, with a jump between each pair. How far is every jump?
How far is each jump? Check every one before you go on.
How many letters does it jump? Jump the same again.
Put them in pairs. Is anyone left without a partner?
The jumps are not the same. Where does each jump come from?
Another track. Check every jump before you fill a stone.
Free play. Choose a start and a rule, and watch the track fill.
Label each jump again from the left, and look for the one that differs.
Every jump labelled, and every series carried on by its own rule.
